title: Cash, Cards & Payment Apps
description: Cash, debit, credit and payment apps: which to use, and how not to get burned.
wolfLine: Money moves fast now. Make sure it’s going where you meant.

peer-to-peer-payment.definition: Sending money straight from one person to another with an app like Venmo, Zelle or Cash App.
peer-to-peer-payment.example: Paying a friend back $12 for pizza from your phone.

sales-tax.definition: A tax added to the price at the register. In most US states the shelf price doesn’t include it.
sales-tax.example: A $40 jacket with 7% sales tax costs $42.80.

foreign-transaction-fee.definition: An extra charge, often 3%, when you pay in another currency or with a store based abroad.
foreign-transaction-fee.example: Spend $500 on a trip and a 3% fee adds $15.

lessons.title: Ways to Pay
lessons.summary: Cash, debit, credit and apps all move money. Differently.

steps.title: Four ways to pay
steps.body: Cash, debit cards, credit cards and payment apps all move money, but they work differently: whose money it is, how fast it moves, and what protection you get if something goes wrong.

steps.context: A [[credit card]] lets you buy now and pay later. The money is borrowed from the card company, and you get a bill each month.
steps.prompt: You pay $50 with a credit card. Whose money paid the store?
choices: The card company’s, and now you owe it back
steps.explain: A credit card is a loan you pay back when the bill comes.

steps.prompt: Whose money is it?
items: Payment app linked to your bank account

steps.prompt: Paying with a credit card always costs the same as paying with a debit card.
steps.explain: Not if you leave part of the bill unpaid. Then you pay interest on top.

steps.prompt: Which way of paying leaves no record unless you write it down?
steps.explain: Cash leaves no trail.

steps.prompt: Match each way to pay.
pairs: Paper money, gone when it’s spent
Sends money between people from your phone

steps.prompt: A thief spends $500 with your stolen card. With which card is your own money missing while the bank investigates?
steps.explain: Debit fraud takes your real cash until it’s sorted out. Credit card fraud is the card company’s money.

steps.prompt: If you pay your credit card bill in full every month, you pay no interest.
steps.explain: Pay in full, and the borrowing is free.

steps.context: If you don’t pay the bill in full, the card charges interest on what’s left. Rates around 24% a year are common.
steps.prompt: You leave $500 unpaid on a card charging about 24% a year. Roughly how much interest is that over a year?
Which habit is safest for a beginner?
choices: Only put on credit what you could pay with cash today, then pay in full
Use credit for things you can’t afford yet
Pay just the minimum each month
steps.explain: Treat it like a debit card that sends one bill.

steps.prompt: Which card builds a credit history?
steps.explain: Credit history comes from borrowing and paying back on time. More on that in the Credit & Debt section.

steps.prompt: With a ___ card, the money comes straight out of your checking account.
steps.explain: Debit means your own money.

lessons.title: Payment Apps
lessons.summary: Instant and easy. Also instant and final.

steps.context: A [[peer-to-peer payment]] app (like Venmo, Zelle or Cash App) sends money from one person to another in seconds.
steps.prompt: What’s a payment app best for?
choices: Paying back a friend you know
Paying someone who says you won a prize
steps.explain: Use it with people you know and trust.

steps.prompt: If you send money to the wrong person on a payment app, you can always get it back.
steps.explain: Payments are often instant and final. Check the name and number before you hit send.

steps.prompt: Before sending $60 to a friend, what should you check?
choices: Their exact name or number, and the amount
steps.explain: One wrong digit sends your money to a stranger.

steps.prompt: A stranger “accidentally” sends you $200 and asks you to send it back. What’s going on?
choices: Probably a scam: their $200 may vanish later, and yours won’t come back
steps.explain: Tell them to ask their bank to reverse it. Don’t send your own money.

steps.prompt: An instant transfer to your bank costs 1.75%. How much is that on $400?
Money sitting in a payment app balance may not have FDIC insurance.
steps.explain: Many app balances aren’t bank deposits. Move larger amounts to your insured account.

lessons.title: Tips & Sales Tax
lessons.summary: The price on the tag isn’t the price you pay.

steps.context: [[Sales tax]] is added at the register in most US states. The price on the tag usually doesn’t include it.
steps.prompt: A $40 jacket with 7% sales tax. What do you pay?
8.25% sales tax on a $200 purchase. How much is the tax?
Where do US prices usually include sales tax already?
choices: Hardly anywhere, so add it in your head
steps.explain: Expect the register total to be a bit higher than the tag.

steps.context: To work out a tip, multiply. 20% is the same as × 0.20.
steps.prompt: What’s a 20% tip on a $45 meal?
What’s a 15% tip on $60?
A quick way to find 20%: find 10% by moving the decimal point one place left, then double it.
steps.explain: 10% of $45 is $4.50. Double it: $9.

lessons.title: Splitting the Bill
lessons.summary: Dinner for two: tax, tip and who owes what.

steps.prompt: What’s the total before tip?
steps.explain: It’s printed at the bottom: $80.46.

steps.context: Tip is usually worked out on the total before tax, often 18–20%.
steps.prompt: A 20% tip on the $74.50 subtotal?
You split the total plus tip evenly between 2 friends. What does each pay?
You had the salad and one lemonade. Your friend had everything else. What’s the fairest split?
choices: Each pays for what they ordered
steps.explain: Even splits are easy, but item-by-item is fair when orders are lopsided.

steps.prompt: Your items: the salad and one $4.50 lemonade. What’s your subtotal?
When you split by item, tax and tip should be shared in the same proportion.
steps.explain: You ordered about 22% of the food, so you cover about 22% of the tax and tip.

lessons.title: Cash Still Counts
lessons.summary: Why paper money still has a place.

steps.context: Paying with cash feels different. Handing over real bills makes spending more noticeable, so many people spend less.
steps.prompt: Why do some people budget with cash?
choices: It’s harder to overspend money you can see
Every store gives a cash discount
steps.explain: Watching the bills leave your hand makes spending feel real.

steps.prompt: Some stores and gas stations charge less if you pay with cash.
steps.explain: Card fees cost them money, so some pass the saving on.

steps.context: At many stores you can ask for cash back at the register when you pay with debit, usually with no fee.
steps.prompt: You need $40 in cash. Cheapest way?
choices: Cash back at the grocery register with your debit card
An out-of-network ATM with two fees
steps.explain: Many stores give cash back with a debit purchase for free.

steps.prompt: Your weekly cash budget is $80. You’ve spent $23, $18 and $27. How much is left?
What’s the downside of cash?
choices: If it’s lost or stolen, it’s gone
steps.explain: No fraud protection, no getting it back.

steps.prompt: A cash week: put it in order.
items: Spend only what’s in your wallet
Note what’s left at the end of the week
steps.explain: Plan, withdraw, spend, review.

lessons.title: Request or Scam?
lessons.summary: Payment apps are a scammer’s favorite tool. Spot the setup.

steps.context: Scammers love payment apps because money moves instantly and is hard to get back.
steps.prompt: Tap the request you should decline.
steps.explain: A real prize never charges a fee to “release” it.

steps.prompt: Why is a “release fee” for a prize a red flag?
choices: Real prizes don’t make you pay to collect them
steps.explain: If you have to pay to win, you didn’t win.

steps.prompt: Payment app scammers often pretend to be your bank, a store, or someone you know.
steps.explain: Check by calling the real person or company yourself.

steps.prompt: Someone selling concert tickets online wants payment through an app. What’s safer?
choices: Buy through a platform with buyer protection, or pay by credit card
steps.explain: Payment apps rarely protect purchases from strangers.

steps.prompt: You think you’ve been scammed on an app. Put it in order.
steps.explain: Fast reports give you the best chance of getting money back.

steps.prompt: Who should you send money to with a payment app?
steps.explain: Treat it like handing over cash.

lessons.title: Paying Online & Abroad
lessons.summary: Hidden fees on trips and risky checkouts.

steps.context: A [[foreign transaction fee]] is an extra charge, often 3%, when you pay in another currency or with a store based abroad.
steps.prompt: You spend $500 abroad on a card with a 3% foreign transaction fee. How much is the fee?
A card machine abroad asks: pay in dollars or local currency?
choices: Local currency, to avoid the machine’s worse exchange rate
steps.explain: Paying in dollars lets the shop pick the exchange rate, and it’s rarely a good one.

steps.prompt: Shopping online, what makes a site safer?
choices: A store you know, a secure checkout, and paying by credit card
steps.explain: Too-good deals and pop-ups are classic warning signs.

steps.prompt: Saving your card on lots of small websites is low risk.
steps.explain: Every site that stores your card is another place it can leak.

steps.prompt: A trip costs $1,200 on a card with a 3% foreign transaction fee. What’s the fee?
Which card is best for travel?
choices: One with no foreign transaction fee
The one with the nicest design
A debit card with ATM fees
steps.explain: Many cards charge 0%. Check before you go.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Ways to Pay
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: What’s a 20% tip on a $35 meal?
Your card is stolen and used. Which card keeps your own cash safe while the bank investigates?
steps.explain: With credit, it’s the card company’s money on the line.

steps.prompt: Payments sent on a peer-to-peer app are easy to reverse.
steps.explain: They’re usually instant and final.

steps.prompt: 6% sales tax on a $150 purchase. How much is the tax?
